text: Given a string s, return the longest substring that is a palindrome — one that reads the same forwards and backwards.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — substring means contiguous, not a subsequence. If there are ties in length, any one is fine? And the length is up to about a thousand?
Correct on all three — contiguous, any longest one is fine, and n is at most a thousand.
Let me run through an example: babad. B-a-b is a palindrome of length three; so is a-b-a. Nothing longer works, so the answer is b-a-b, or a-b-a.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. Checking every substring is n squared substrings times linear time to verify each — cubic, too slow. The key structure: a palindrome with its two ends peeled off is still a palindrome. This problem reminds me of interval DP, because that peel-the-ends rule is a recurrence over ranges: dp of i, j means s from i to j is a palindrome, and it depends only on the range one step inside. There's also expand-around-center with constant space — I'll mention it after.

Here's the plan. One: every single character is a palindrome, and a pair is one when its two characters match. Two: for length three and up, i to j is a palindrome when the end characters match and the inside, i plus one to j minus one, is a palindrome. Three: fill by length, ascending, and track the longest as a start and a length. One thing worth flagging — the outer loop must run over length, not over i and j. The inner cell is two shorter, so all shorter lengths must be done first. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code the DP, and show the expand-around-center variant too.

Alright, let me code this up — the interval DP first. Base loops mark lengths one and two; then the outer loop walks length L from three up, and the inner loop slides the window. Every time a cell turns true I set the answer to its start and length; since lengths only grow, the last update is the longest. Then expand-around-center — same quadratic time, but constant space. One thing worth flagging — expand needs two centers per index: c with c for odd lengths, c with c plus one for even, or you miss palindromes like b-b. And when the loop stops, left and right have each overshot by one, so the length is right minus left minus one.

Let's dry-run the DP on abba, expected abba. Length one is all true, and length two finds b-b in the middle. Length three fails on both windows. The row that matters is length four: the outer a's match, and the inner cell, b-b, was already computed back at length two — so the whole string is true, and the answer is abba. That matches. Corner cases: cbbd returns b-b, through the even base case; a single character like a returns itself.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is quadratic for both. Space is quadratic for the DP table, constant for expand-around-center. Oh, one more thing — the same dp table also solves counting palindromic substrings: just increment a counter on every true cell instead of tracking the longest. And if n were up to ten to the fifth, I'd reach for Manacher's algorithm, which is truly linear.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You used the peel-the-ends recurrence and filled by length, so the inner cell is always ready. You gave the constant-space expand variant with both odd and even centers. And you connected the table to counting palindromes and to Manacher. Good work.
